notes: Place-anchored subset: canon rows of kind place, maker community and institution, geocoded at build time; world-set objects at their holders; route stops; the Edo case.

Geocoding: an exact Natural Earth populated-place name inside the row’s own sub-regions (public domain), else an exact Pleiades title (CC BY 3.0), else a city named in the record, else the sub-region as a soft blot. Proposals, not confirmed identifications: a person should review them as the register does for Wikidata ids.
Territories: Natural Earth admin-0 shapes grouped by the canon’s sub-region codes; a chapter’s wash is densest where its canon rows are. A reading, not a border.
Routes: schematic great-circle paths through named nodes; never surveyed tracks.

units.title: One object, three readings: material, labour, meaning
units.summary: A clay account of barley can be read three ways: what it is made of, who worked on it, and what it meant. Each reading pulls a different strand of the web.
units.question: What can one object tell you about the people around it, and what does each way of reading it leave out?

units.title: The reference-to-appropriation plane
units.summary: Every borrowing sits somewhere on two separate scales: how much of the source it takes, and how much harm it does to the people it came from.
units.question: When one maker uses another people's form, what decides whether it is a nod, a copy, a trade good or a taking?

units.title: How histories get written: canons, periods, the timeline as an argument; design history versus design studies
units.summary: Every design timeline makes an argument about who counts, and someone made it at a known date. The learner learns to read a canon, a period and a civilisation label as claims by a source, and to annotate what they leave out.
units.question: Who decided where design history starts, how it is cut into periods, and who is in it?

units.title: Interdisciplinary discourse: film, performance, sound, gaming and digital culture as teachers of making
units.summary: Films, recordings, games and performances are made things, and each holds a method a designer can take into another world.
units.question: What can a maker learn about making from a film, a recording, a game or a performance?

units.title: Recurrences
units.summary: Writing, pottery, metals, cities, cotton and printing each began more than once; a "first" is a claim about what survived.
units.question: How many times did people begin to write, fire clay, smelt metal, build cities, grow cotton and print, and how would you know?

units.title: Africa, read through metallurgy
units.summary: Read through metal, Africa's making is a set of inventions and exchanges on its own terms, and how each object reached a museum is part of what it teaches.
units.question: Whose metal is this, who worked it, and how do we know?

units.title: The Americas, read through fibre
units.summary: We read the Americas through fibre: in the Andes, dyed cotton cloth is the earliest known craft on record, and across the hemisphere cloth and cord carried rank, tribute and accounts.
units.question: What did fibre hold in the Americas (value, rank, tribute, a record), and what do the records of each cloth leave out?

units.title: East Asia, read through the workshop
units.summary: East Asia's best-recorded objects can be read as the work of organised groups making to written standards, and the records show who counted the hands and who left them out.
units.question: Who made this object, how many hands did it pass through, and who wrote down the count?

units.title: South and Southeast Asia, read through cotton
units.summary: Indian cloth was worn from Cairo to Maluku, and its records say where it ended up more often than who made it.
units.question: Where was this cloth made, who made it, and how do we know when the record says where it was found?

units.title: West Asia before Islam, read through the account
units.summary: West Asia holds the earliest securely dated records of making, and each record, like each object's own paper trail, counts some hands and leaves others out.
units.question: What did people in West Asia write down about making, and who does each account count, name or leave out?

units.title: The Islamic world as a network, read through routes and the waqf
units.summary: We read the Islamic world as a network: routes moved paper, cobalt, cloth, skills and people, and endowments paid makers to build and keep things working.
units.question: What moved along the routes of the Islamic world, who paid for what was made, and who kept it working?

units.title: Europe and the Mediterranean, read through the guild
units.summary: Europe is one world of making among several, and its guild rules show who was let in to make and who was kept out.
units.question: Who was allowed to make this, who wrote the rule, and whom did the rule keep out?

units.title: Australia and the Pacific, read through navigation
units.summary: We read Australia and the Pacific through navigation: knowledge of sea, stone and water, held in memory and practice and carried in canoes.
units.question: What did makers here hold in memory, stone and canoe, and who may tell it now?

units.title: The steppe and Central Asia, read through the horse
units.summary: We read the steppe through the horse (what it needed made, what it made possible, what was made from it), and the chapter's best-known "first" is still argued.
units.question: What did people on the steppe make for, with and from the horse, and how sure is the record of where the horse story begins?

units.title: Networks: objects, materials, skills and people
units.summary: A network is four flows at once (objects, materials, skills and people), and this unit follows one jar's blue through all four.
units.question: What moved along a route (an object, a material, a skill or a person), who moved it, and on what terms?
units.layerDoes: Lights the routes: every major route inks at full strength.

units.title: Copying, transfer and counterfeit
units.summary: Copying is how making has always travelled; it turns into theft when a mark lies, a market is taken without return, or nothing new is made, and who draws that line has changed with every century.
units.question: When does a copy make something new, and when does it take what belongs to another maker?

units.title: Ornament as a global language; the exhibition as taxonomy
units.summary: Patterns are related by how they were made, by who met whom, or by who displayed them together, and the museum record shows which.
units.question: When two patterns from different worlds look alike, who decided they belong together: the makers, or the people who printed, exhibited and catalogued them?

units.title: Ritual and belief as drivers of making
units.summary: Belief drives making through who commissions, what a rite requires, how often it repeats, where pilgrims spend and who reorganises the workshop; this unit follows those drivers, not theology.
units.question: When a rite or a belief asks for an object, what changes in who pays, who makes, how many, and by what rule?

units.title: Who commissions: patrons, guilds, merchants, industry, agencies, platforms
units.summary: Someone has always written the brief, and across six regimes the brief, the money and the credit have separated and recombined.
units.question: Who has told makers what to make, and how did the brief change hands across history?

units.title: Textiles and the making called women's work; women's making beyond textiles
units.summary: Institutions put women at the loom and the kiln, and credit lines then decided whose hands the record kept.
units.question: Who decided that this making was "women's work", and whose names did the record keep?

units.title: Industry, the machine and the exhibition
units.summary: The machine changed who did each step of making, how fast, from what material and for whose credit, and it did so differently in Lyon, Dhaka, Kyoto and the Gold Coast.
units.question: When a machine enters a craft, which steps does it take, who loses or gains the work, and what stays in the hand?
units.layerDoes: Marks the exhibition cities, once, with a ring.

units.title: War, crisis and making: rationing, military production, reconstruction, propaganda, displacement
units.summary: War does not stop making; it changes who pays, what is allowed, what the message says and where makers are forced to live, and this unit counts the people in that ledger before it counts any design.
units.question: When a war or a crisis arrives, what happens to a maker's patron, materials, message and home, and who pays for the change?

units.title: The designer: how making split into designing, and how it was taught
units.summary: Designing became a separate job when workshops, then schools, taught some people to draw what others would make; every learner inherits one of those methods, knowingly or not.
units.question: When did drawing the thing become a different job from making it, who was taught to do it, and whose method is inside your own training?

units.title: Modernisms, plural
units.summary: Modernism was made in many centres, for revolutions, empires and new nations; this unit sets those modernisms side by side, not on one line with provinces.
units.question: When a state, a school or a new nation said "modern", what did it take from the past, what did it refuse, and who made the things?

units.title: Consumer society, the digital and the platform
units.summary: Every age of buying has a counter that sets the terms between maker and buyer, from the Edo cloth shop to the platform, and the maker's name, script and share are decided there.
units.question: Who sets the terms between the person who makes a thing and the person who buys it, and what does a maker lose or gain at each new counter?

units.title: The planetary present: making as extraction
units.summary: Every made thing starts in a place that gave something up; this unit maps who dug, grew or carried it, what the place lost, and who counted the loss.
units.question: What did one object take, from which places and from whose work, and who counted it?
units.layerDoes: Runs extraction flows from source to city.

units.title: Use and consumption: how things were lived with, worn out, repaired, resold, inherited
units.summary: An object's history does not stop when its maker lets go: use, wear, repair, resale and inheritance leave marks, and those marks are evidence.
units.question: What happened to this object after it left its maker, who did it, and what marks did that life leave?

units.title: Obscured labour: the credit map
units.summary: The name on an object usually belongs to whoever owned, ruled or sold, and the hands that made it were left off by law, force or habit.
units.question: Whose name is on this object, who made it, and what kept the makers' names off it?

units.title: The museum as author: collecting, provenance, restitution
units.summary: A museum authors an object's second life through what it collects, records and returns, and every link it writes can be checked.
units.question: Who writes an object's story after it leaves its makers, and how do you check what they wrote?
units.layerDoes: Draws provenance arcs from where things were made to where they are held now: a reverse route.

units.title: Reading an object as history: slow looking and the autopsy
units.summary: An object read slowly, in five layers (material, technique, labour, trade, meaning), shows a web of hands and routes; its museum record is one more source, with its own authors and gaps.
units.question: How much of an object's history can you read from the thing itself, and how much comes from a record someone else wrote?

units.title: Attribution and consultation as protocol, on the CARE principles
units.summary: Credit given after an outcry is repair; a protocol is the set of steps you run before the work, and every step leaves a record.
units.question: Before you use another people's form, whom do you ask, through whom, and what do you write down?

units.title: Counter-history research piece on one lineage
units.summary: A lineage is a set of links someone drew; a counter-history redraws them one link at a time, with a source and a confidence for each.
units.question: Who drew the line you were taught for your lineage, when did they draw it, and what does it leave out?

units.title: Primary sources and archives
units.summary: A primary source carries who wrote it, for whom, in which language and through whose hands, so grading it means reading those layers before its content.
units.question: What can this source carry, and what has been added between its writer and you?

units.title: Reconstruction: making to know
units.summary: Remaking a technique from a text, an object or a holder's account shows what the record left unsaid, and the result is an interpretation that must say what was decided.
units.question: What does making something again teach that reading about it cannot, and how do you keep the remake from passing as evidence?

units.title: Vernacular intelligence: oral history, folktale, local taxonomy, with consent
units.summary: What people say, tell and name about making is evidence, and it reaches the record only on their terms.
units.question: How do you record what people know about making without taking it from them?

units.title: Re-timing the Atlas: other calendars and periodisations
units.summary: Every date in the Atlas began in some calendar, and someone converted it to "CE". The learner puts their own lineage on another calendar and records what each conversion kept, widened or lost.
units.question: When a date moves from one calendar to another, what changes, and who chose the calendar in the first place?
units.layerDoes: Relabels the time scrubber in another calendar: Japanese era names (nengō) or the Hijri era.

units.title: Counterfactual history: a history of making that did not happen
units.summary: Change one fact about the past, trace what follows through sources, and label the result fiction: done this way, a "what if" tests which causes a history of making really rests on, and it can seed a world.
units.question: If one fact in a history of making changed, what would follow, and how would you know which parts you invented?

units.title: Regional slot: the learner's own place, authored locally
units.summary: The program builds the frame for a place's history of making, and the people who hold that history write it; this unit specifies the frame, the authorship rules and the review, and leaves the content empty.
units.question: Who has the standing to write the history of making of a place, and what must the record show for others to trust it?

lenses.name: Labour and credit
lenses.q: Who did the work, and whose name stayed on it?
lenses.rule: Maker communities and guilds; rows whose text names workers, wages, crews or unnamed hands; routes that moved people.

lenses.name: Material and extraction
lenses.q: Where did the material come from, and what did that place give up?
lenses.rule: Mines, quarries and source places; routes that carried raw materials; extraction flows.

lenses.name: Gender
lenses.q: Whose making was called women’s work, and who left women out of the record?
lenses.rule: Rows whose making or whose silences name women.

lenses.name: Ritual and belief
lenses.q: What was this made for beyond use?
lenses.rule: Rows with the function “ritual and belief” or a sacred flag.

lenses.name: Commissioning
lenses.q: Who ordered this, and on what terms?
lenses.rule: Rows with the function “rule and display”, or that name a court, patron or commission.

lenses.name: Copying and transfer
lenses.q: What was copied, by whom, and was anything returned?
lenses.rule: Rows that name copies, imitation or transfer; copy threads.

lenses.name: Provenance and restitution
lenses.q: How did it leave, and who asks for it back?
lenses.rule: Rows flagged for conflict or looting, or naming removal, collecting or return; provenance arcs.

routes.name: Silk Roads
routes.label: Silk Roads
routes.m: Relay routes across Eurasia carried silk, paper-making, glass, metalwork, textile patterns, pigments and travelling craftspeople between China, Central Asia, Iran, South Asia and the Mediterranean.
routes.o: The name privileges silk and the two ends; it leaves out steppe herders, oasis makers, non-silk goods, and the relay character of most exchange.
routes.d: conventional start with Han envoy Zhang Qian's missions c.138–126 BCE; steppe exchange far older; decline after c.1450 debated

routes.name: Steppe route
routes.label: Steppe route
routes.m: Mobile pastoralists moved horse gear, chariot technology, bronze metallurgy, felt and gold animal-style ornament across the grasslands from Hungary to Mongolia.
routes.o: Framing as 'route' can hide that herders were makers and patrons, not only carriers.
routes.d: east–west movement of horses, chariots and metallurgy from the 3rd–2nd millennium BCE; Mongol-era (13th–14th c.) peak; ongoing in altered form

routes.name: Oasis route (Tarim Basin)
routes.label: Oasis route (Tarim Basin)
routes.m: Oasis cities such as Dunhuang, Turfan, Kucha, Khotan and Kashgar were workshops and relay points for silk, jade, wall painting, manuscripts and Buddhist image-making.
routes.o: The early-20th-c. removals of Dunhuang and Turfan material to European and Japanese collections are part of this history.
routes.d: Han to late first millennium CE; approximate

routes.name: Tea Horse Road
routes.label: Tea Horse Road
routes.m: Mule caravans and human porters carried compressed brick tea from Yunnan and Sichuan to Tibet in exchange for horses, wool and medicinal goods.
routes.o: Porters' labour (many carried loads over 100 kg) is rarely centred.
routes.d: Song-dynasty tea-for-horses trade formalised 11th c.; Tang origins claimed; porterage into the 20th c.

routes.name: Indian Ocean world
routes.label: Indian Ocean world
routes.m: Monsoon-timed sailing linked textile, bead, ceramic and metal makers from East Africa to China, spreading cotton cloth, glass beads, stoneware and shipbuilding know-how.
routes.o: Enslaved people moved through the same circuits; coastal and island makers are often reduced to entrepôts.
routes.d: from Harappan–Gulf contact c.2500 BCE; monsoon sailing documented by 1st c. CE; ongoing

routes.name: Arabian Sea circuit
routes.label: Arabian Sea circuit
routes.m: The western Indian Ocean circuit moved Gujarati and Malabar textiles, pepper, beads, incense and Chinese ceramics between India, Arabia, the Red Sea and East Africa.
routes.d: Harappan–Gulf phase c.2500 BCE; Periplus of the Erythraean Sea 1st c. CE; ongoing

routes.name: Bay of Bengal circuit
routes.label: Bay of Bengal circuit
routes.m: Exchange between eastern India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia carried glass and stone beads, rouletted ware, Buddhist and Hindu image-making and textile patterns.
routes.o: South Asian craftspeople working in Southeast Asian ports.
routes.d: Khao Sam Kaeo and Arikamedu evidence from 4th–1st c. BCE; ongoing

routes.name: Nanhai route
routes.label: Nanhai route
routes.m: Chinese ports shipped stoneware, porcelain, silk and iron to the south and west; wrecks such as Belitung (c.830) and Nanhai One (12th c.) preserve whole cargoes.
routes.d: Han references; Song–Yuan peak at Guangzhou and Quanzhou

routes.name: Trans-Saharan trade
routes.label: Trans-Saharan trade
routes.m: Camel caravans exchanged West African gold, salt, copper, glass, textiles and books, and carried Maghribi and Sahelian styles of building, leatherwork and manuscript making.
routes.o: Enslaved people were moved across the Sahara; Tuareg and Sahelian makers.
routes.d: camel caravans from c.3rd–4th c. CE; earlier Garamantian links; decline late 19th c.

routes.name: Trans-Saharan trade
routes.label: Trans-Saharan trade
routes.m: Camel caravans exchanged West African gold, salt, copper, glass, textiles and books, and carried Maghribi and Sahelian styles of building, leatherwork and manuscript making.
routes.o: Enslaved people were moved across the Sahara; Tuareg and Sahelian makers.
routes.d: camel caravans from c.3rd–4th c. CE; earlier Garamantian links; decline late 19th c.

routes.name: Kilwa gold route
routes.label: Kilwa gold route
routes.m: Gold from the Zimbabwe Plateau passed through Sofala to Kilwa, financing coral-stone building and coinage and bringing Chinese porcelain and Indian beads inland.
routes.o: Local miners and Shona-speaking makers are often subordinated to coastal narratives.
routes.d: Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe periods; approximate

routes.name: Swahili dhow trade
routes.label: Swahili dhow trade
routes.m: Monsoon dhows moved mangrove poles, ivory, textiles, carved doors and ceramics between the East African coast, Arabia and India, and carried boat-building skills.
routes.o: 19th-c. trafficking of enslaved people through Zanzibar.
routes.d: from c.8th c.; ongoing on a small scale (Lamu, Zanzibar)

routes.name: Dilmun–Magan–Meluhha trade
routes.label: Dilmun–Magan–Meluhha trade
routes.m: Maritime trade brought Magan copper, Indus carnelian beads and seals, and timber to Mesopotamia, recorded in cuneiform and seen in Ur's royal tombs.
routes.o: Identification of Meluhha with the Indus region is a scholarly consensus, not a self-name.
routes.d: Akkadian texts name Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (the Oman peninsula, today Oman and the UAE) and Meluhha (Indus region)

routes.name: Old Assyrian trade (Aššur–Kaneš)
routes.label: Old Assyrian trade (Aššur–Kaneš)
routes.m: Assyrian merchant families shipped tin and textiles by donkey caravan to Anatolia for silver and gold, documented in some 23,000 cuneiform letters.
routes.o: Assyrian women who wove textiles for export and wrote letters.
routes.d: Kültepe (Kaneš) level II and Ib

routes.name: Lapis lazuli route
routes.label: Lapis lazuli route
routes.m: Lapis lazuli from Sar-i Sang in Badakhshan reached Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Indus, where it was carved into beads, inlays and seals.
routes.d: lapis in Mehrgarh earlier; Mesopotamian and Egyptian use from 4th millennium BCE

routes.name: Anatolian obsidian network
routes.label: Anatolian obsidian network
routes.m: Obsidian from Göllü Dağ and Nenezi Dağ in Cappadocia travelled to the Levant and Cyprus as blades, cores and mirrors (Çatalhöyük).
routes.d: Epipalaeolithic to Chalcolithic; approximate

routes.name: Late Bronze Age Eastern Mediterranean exchange
routes.label: Late Bronze Age Eastern Mediterranean exchange
routes.m: Palace and merchant trade moved copper oxhide ingots, tin, glass ingots, ebony, ivory and textiles between Egypt, Cyprus, the Levant, Anatolia and the Aegean, as shown by the Uluburun wreck.
routes.o: Nubian gold and ebony producers.
routes.d: 'Bronze Age' as defined for the Aegean and Near East

routes.name: Phoenician network
routes.label: Phoenician network
routes.m: Phoenician cities and colonies carried purple-dyed cloth, carved ivory, metal bowls, glass and the alphabet across the Mediterranean to Iberia and North Africa.
routes.o: 'Phoenician' is a Greek name; the people called themselves by city (e.g. Tyrians).
routes.d: Iron Age; to fall of Carthage 146 BCE

routes.name: Roman Mediterranean trade
routes.label: Roman Mediterranean trade
routes.m: Roman shipping standardised amphorae, terra sigillata, marble, glass and grain across the Mediterranean and linked it to the Red Sea and India.
routes.o: Enslaved workers produced and moved much of this trade.
routes.d: approximate

routes.name: Medieval Mediterranean trade
routes.label: Medieval Mediterranean trade
routes.m: Islamic, Byzantine and Italian traders moved silks, lustreware, paper, glass, alum and sugar between the Levant, Egypt, the Maghrib, Iberia and Italy.
routes.d: approximate

routes.name: Venetian and Genoese trade networks
routes.label: Venetian and Genoese trade networks
routes.m: Venetian and Genoese colonies from Crete to Caffa moved silks, alum, spices and glass, and supported Murano glass and Italian silk weaving.
routes.o: Genoese trafficking of enslaved people via Caffa and Black Sea ports.
routes.d: Byzantine privileges for Venice 1082; Venice falls 1797; Genoese colonies to 15th–16th c.

routes.name: Amber Road
routes.label: Amber Road
routes.m: Baltic amber moved south to Mycenaean Greece, Etruria and Roman Aquileia, where it was carved into beads, pendants and figures.
routes.d: Baltic amber in Mycenaean graves from c.1600 BCE; Roman Aquileia trade

routes.name: Varangian route
routes.label: Varangian route
routes.m: Scandinavian traders moved along the Dnieper to Constantinople, exchanging furs, wax and enslaved people for silk, silver and glass.
routes.o: Slavic, Finnic and Baltic peoples along the rivers.
routes.d: approximate

routes.name: Volga trade route
routes.label: Volga trade route
routes.m: Islamic silver dirhams flowed north via the Volga for furs, wax and enslaved people, filling Scandinavian and Baltic hoards.
routes.o: Volga Bulgars and Khazars as intermediaries.
routes.d: approximate

routes.name: Hanseatic League
routes.label: Hanseatic League
routes.m: A league of merchant towns ran kontore in Bergen, London, Bruges and Novgorod, moving stockfish, furs, wax, cloth and amber in cog ships.
routes.d: Lübeck refounded 1159; last Hanseatic diet 1669

routes.name: Grand Trunk Road
routes.label: Grand Trunk Road
routes.m: A trunk road from Bengal to Kabul carried goods, armies and craftspeople and was punctuated by serais, kos minars and wells.
routes.d: Mauryan route; rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri 1540s; ongoing

routes.name: Incense routes
routes.label: Incense routes
routes.m: Caravans carried frankincense and myrrh from South Arabia and the Horn to the Mediterranean, funding Nabataean building at Petra and in the Negev.
routes.o: Harvesters in Dhofar and Somaliland.
routes.d: approximate

routes.name: Red Sea network
routes.label: Red Sea network
routes.m: Red Sea harbours linked Egypt, Aksum and Arabia to the Indian Ocean, carrying incense, ivory, glass, textiles and pepper.
routes.d: Egyptian harbour at Wadi al-Jarf c.2600 BCE; Punt voyages; Berenike and Aksum; ongoing

routes.name: Cape Route and the East India companies
routes.label: Dutch East India Company ships, Amsterdam to Nagasaki
routes.m: Chartered companies shipped Asian textiles, porcelain, lacquer and spices to Europe and commissioned designs for European taste.
routes.o: Company slave trading (e.g. VOC to the Cape) and colonial coercion.
routes.d: da Gama 1498; VOC 1602–1799; English EIC to 1874

routes.name: Cape Route and the East India companies
routes.label: Cape Route and the East India companies
routes.m: Chartered companies shipped Asian textiles, porcelain, lacquer and spices to Europe and commissioned designs for European taste.
routes.o: Company slave trading (e.g. VOC to the Cape) and colonial coercion.
routes.d: da Gama 1498; VOC 1602–1799; English EIC to 1874

routes.name: Atlantic world trade
routes.label: Atlantic world trade
routes.m: Atlantic shipping moved plants, animals, metals, dyes and manufactured goods between Europe, Africa and the Americas, reshaping materials available to makers on all three continents.
routes.o: Indigenous dispossession and forced labour; enslaved Africans (see separate node).
routes.d: approximate

routes.name: Transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans
routes.label: Forced passage: Bight of Benin to Bahia (schematic)
routes.m: About 12.5 million African people were forcibly embarked; their knowledge of rice cultivation, indigo, ironworking, textiles, building and music shaped making across the Americas.
routes.o: People are shown as people, never as goods; content note required.
routes.d: first direct Africa–Americas voyage c.1525; last documented voyage 1866–67

routes.name: Transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans
routes.label: Forced passage: West Central Africa to Brazil (schematic)
routes.m: About 12.5 million African people were forcibly embarked; their knowledge of rice cultivation, indigo, ironworking, textiles, building and music shaped making across the Americas.
routes.o: People are shown as people, never as goods; content note required.
routes.d: first direct Africa–Americas voyage c.1525; last documented voyage 1866–67

routes.name: Manila galleon trade
routes.label: Manila galleon trade
routes.m: Galleons carried Mexican and Peruvian silver to Manila and Chinese silk, porcelain, lacquer and ivory to Acapulco, prompting enconchado painting, Puebla talavera and biombos.
routes.o: Enslaved and indentured Asians ('chinos') carried to New Spain.
routes.d: first return voyage 1565; last galleon 1815

routes.name: Manila galleon trade
routes.label: Manila galleon trade
routes.m: Galleons carried Mexican and Peruvian silver to Manila and Chinese silk, porcelain, lacquer and ivory to Acapulco, prompting enconchado painting, Puebla talavera and biombos.
routes.o: Enslaved and indentured Asians ('chinos') carried to New Spain.
routes.d: first return voyage 1565; last galleon 1815

routes.name: Mesoamerican obsidian network
routes.label: Mesoamerican obsidian network
routes.m: Obsidian from sources such as Pachuca, El Chayal and Ixtepeque moved as cores and prismatic blades, supporting workshops at Teotihuacan and across the Maya region.
routes.d: Formative to Spanish conquest; approximate

routes.name: Southwest–Mesoamerica turquoise networks
routes.label: Southwest–Mesoamerica turquoise networks
routes.m: Turquoise from mines such as Cerrillos was worked into mosaics in the Southwest; long-distance supply to Mesoamerica is now contested.
routes.o: Recent isotope work suggests Aztec turquoise came mainly from Mesoamerican sources.
routes.d: approximate

routes.name: Qhapaq Ñan
routes.label: Qhapaq Ñan
routes.m: An Inca network of roughly 30,000 km with tambos, storehouses and fibre suspension bridges moved goods, cloth tribute and messengers across the Andes.
routes.o: Communities rebuild the Q'eswachaka bridge annually.
routes.d: Inca incorporation of earlier roads; approximate

routes.name: Austronesian voyaging
routes.label: Austronesian voyaging
routes.m: Outrigger and double-hulled voyaging carried people, plants, pottery, barkcloth, weaving and wayfinding knowledge from Taiwan to Madagascar and Rapa Nui.
routes.o: Present-day voyaging revival (e.g. Hōkūleʻa, 1976–).
routes.d: out of Taiwan c.3000–2500 BCE; Madagascar c.500–700 CE; Aotearoa c.1250–1300

routes.name: Austronesian voyaging
routes.label: Austronesian voyaging
routes.m: Outrigger and double-hulled voyaging carried people, plants, pottery, barkcloth, weaving and wayfinding knowledge from Taiwan to Madagascar and Rapa Nui.
routes.o: Present-day voyaging revival (e.g. Hōkūleʻa, 1976–).
routes.d: out of Taiwan c.3000–2500 BCE; Madagascar c.500–700 CE; Aotearoa c.1250–1300

routes.name: Lapita exchange network
routes.label: Lapita exchange network
routes.m: Lapita potters made dentate-stamped vessels and moved Talasea obsidian from New Britain as far as Fiji.
routes.o: 'Lapita' is an archaeologists' name from a site.
routes.d: approximate

routes.name: Macassan trepang trade
routes.label: Macassan trepang trade
routes.m: Fleets from Makassar harvested trepang on the northern Australian coast, exchanging cloth, metal and dugout canoes with Yolŋu and other peoples.
routes.d: start c.1720–1780 debated; banned 1906–07

routes.name: Fur trade
routes.label: Fur trade
routes.m: Furs from North America and Siberia were exchanged for wool blankets, glass beads, metal and firearms, changing Indigenous clothing, beadwork and toolkits.
routes.o: Forced tribute and coerced hunting by Indigenous peoples.
routes.d: Russian Siberian fur tribute from 1580s; HBC from 1670

routes.name: Atlantic cotton economy
routes.label: Atlantic cotton economy
routes.m: Cotton grown by enslaved people in the American South fed Lancashire's mechanised mills, which then exported cheap cloth worldwide.
routes.d: Whitney gin 1793 to US emancipation 1865; approximate

routes.name: Congo Free State rubber extraction
routes.label: Congo Free State rubber extraction
routes.m: Forced collection of wild rubber for bicycle and car tyres was enforced by mutilation and hostage-taking, exposed by campaigners with photographs.
routes.o: Congolese testimony; Alice Seeley Harris's photographs.
routes.d: personal rule of Leopold II 1885–1908

routes.name: Guano and nitrate trade
routes.label: Guano and nitrate trade
routes.m: Seabird guano dug by Chinese indentured workers on the Chincha Islands fertilised European and US farms and is a case study in extraction.
routes.o: Chinese indentured workers; War of the Pacific (1879–84).
routes.d: Peruvian guano boom c.1840–1880; nitrates to 1920s

routes.name: Porcelain trade
routes.label: Porcelain copied: Jingdezhen to Persia, Delft and Meissen
routes.m: Chinese and later Japanese porcelain was made for export in huge quantities, copied in Persia, Delftware and Meissen, and adapted to foreign forms.
routes.o: Kiln workers at Jingdezhen.
routes.d: Changsha ware (Belitung wreck c.830); Jingdezhen export 14th–18th c.; Arita export from 1659; ongoing

routes.name: Indian cotton textile trade
routes.label: Indian cottons, then the calico bans and European imitation
routes.m: Painted and printed Indian cottons were traded from Egypt to Indonesia to Europe, prompting British calico bans (1700, 1721) and European imitation.
routes.o: Indian dyers and painters named in few records.
routes.d: cotton trade attested in the Periplus (1st c. CE); Fustat finds 10th–15th c.; European craze 1600s–1700s

routes.name: Van Gogh’s copies
routes.label: Edo prints copied in Paris, 1887 (Edo unit)
routes.m: Van Gogh’s copies of Edo prints (the Edo unit’s timeline, e1887).

exhibitions.m: Often called the first world's fair, it ranked the goods of nations and colonies in a prefabricated iron-and-glass hall, triggering British design reform.
The fair showed Dutch colonial goods and people, including a Javanese village, and spread batik in the Netherlands.
Indian craftsmen were brought to London to work in view as living exhibits.
Lord Curzon's exhibition showed 'pure' Indian crafts and banned European influence.
The Japanese colonial government displayed Korean 'progress' on the grounds of Gyeongbokgung, demolishing palace buildings to do so.
Colonies built pavilions of products and raw materials and brought craftspeople to work on site.
Loans from the Palace Museum shown at the Royal Academy in London shaped Western canons of Chinese art.
Japan at the Paris exposition (the Edo unit’s timeline, e1867).

PER205.m: The Edo publisher commissioned and sold woodblock prints and books by Utamaro, Sharaku and others.

MKR043.m: Publishers such as Tsutaya Juzaburo commissioned designers and hired carvers and printers, controlling what prints were made and sold.

PER206.m: The Edo artist designed prints and design books such as the Hokusai Manga, which circulated in Europe and fed Japonisme.

MAT054.d: Berlin c.1706; imported to Japan from 1820s
MAT054.m: An early synthetic pigment that reached Japan and coloured Hokusai's Great Wave.

PER207.m: The painter, Hokusai's daughter, worked in his studio and made her own paintings with strong light effects; some works credited to him may be hers.

MOV093.m: Okakura Kakuzo and Ernest Fenollosa defined 'Japanese' painting, using mineral pigments on silk, as a modern category against Western oil painting.

POL183.m: The Tokugawa state regulated dress by status, required daimyo residence in Edo and limited foreign trade to Dejima and Chinese ships.

INS025.m: The VOC's artificial-island trading post in Nagasaki was Japan's main channel for European books, instruments and the porcelain trade.

PLC207.m: Dejima was the only European trading post permitted under Tokugawa rule, shipping Japanese porcelain and lacquer and bringing in books and goods.

INS110.m: The guild's sampling officials controlled the quality of wool cloth and commissioned Rembrandt's "The Syndics" for their hall.

PLC353.m: Amsterdam was the seat of the VOC and WIC and a market for Asian goods, sugar and the trade in enslaved Africans.
